body:
`insight:india-psu-ipo-regime` | confidence: verified | date: 2025-04-27 | tickers: MAZDOCK, RVNL, IRCTC, IRFC, LICI, GRSE

Two contradictory base rates, both true for their window. (1) 2010-2021: ThePrint (May 2022) - shares of about half the PSUs that went public since 2010 traded below IPO price; Quartz (2019) - eight of ten government firms listed since 2017 had lost investors money. PSU IPOs were priced for disinvestment targets, and LIC (May 2022) listed at Rs867 vs Rs949 issue. (2) 2020-2025: a PTI analysis (Apr 2025) found IPO investors in 15 of 18 CPSEs listed over eight years earned 'bumper' gains: Mazagon Dock (2020 issue Rs145) ~+3,700%; RVNL (2019, ~Rs19) ~+1,866%; IRCTC (2019, Rs320) ~+1,110% (only PSU IPO listing at >100% premium); Garden Reach >1,000%; IRFC (2021, Rs26) ~Rs142 in Apr 2025. Laggards were insurers - LIC below issue; GIC Re and New India Assurance negative even after 2018 1:1 bonuses. Drivers of the turn: defence indigenisation and rail capex budgets, dividend yields of 5-8% at 2020-21 lows, single-digit P/Es, then retail/thematic-fund flows. Lesson: ownership type is not destiny; starting valuation + policy tailwind + order book visibility drove returns. Early signal visible in 2020-21: PSU P/E and P/B at multi-decade lows while government capex and import substitution policy were explicit. Risk on the other side: 2024 peak valuations (40-60x P/E for some defence/rail names) reversed sharply. Figures are dated snapshots (2019-2025), adjust for splits/bonuses before reuse.

body:
- **Factoring or receivable discounting without recourse.** The receivable leaves the balance sheet and the cash lands in CFO. Economically it is a loan against your sales.
- **Supplier finance (reverse factoring).** A bank pays your supplier on day 30 and you repay the bank on day 120. Your payables stay "trade payables", and CFO looks better by the stretched amount.
- **Disclosure.** Since FY2023, US GAAP ASU 2022-04 requires companies to disclose supplier-finance obligations. The XBRL tag is `SupplierFinanceProgramObligation`, and 87 filers tagged it at CY2025Q4. IFRS (IAS 7/IFRS 7 amendments, May 2023, effective 2024) now requires similar disclosure. Ind AS has amended Ind AS 7 and 107 to match, so check the "supplier finance arrangements" note in FY26 Indian annual reports.

**Worked example C: Advance Auto Parts (US-AAP). SEC XBRL, 10-K accession 0001193125-26-051305.**

| $ m | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accounts payable | 3,526 | 3,408 | 2,977 |
| of which supplier-finance obligations | **3,400** | 3,200 | 2,500 |
| COGS (continuing) | 5,349 | 5,685 | 4,868 |
| Payable days (AP/COGS×365) | **241** | 219 | 223 |
| Inventory days | 266 | 232 | 273 |
| CFO (total) | 287 | 85 | **−46** |

- About **96%** of FY23 payables sat in a bank programme.
- AAP funded inventory with roughly 8 months of "trade credit" that was bank credit.
- As the programme shrank by $0.9 bn over two years, CFO fell from +$287 m to −$46 m.
- **Lesson:** add supplier-finance obligations to debt when you compute leverage. Treat a programme that is shrinking as a cash outflow coming your way.

title: course › 1.3 Factoring and supply-chain (reverse) finance: CFO that is really debt

body:
| Metric | Formula | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Debtor days (DSO) | Trade receivables / Revenue × 365 | Use average receivables if they are seasonal |
| Inventory days (DIO) | Inventory / COGS × 365 | Screener uses sales when COGS is unavailable, so its figures run lower |
| Payable days (DPO) | Trade payables / COGS (or purchases) × 365 | |
| Cash conversion cycle | DSO + DIO − DPO | |
| **Total DSO (IT/EPC)** | (Receivables + unbilled revenue/contract assets) / Revenue × 365 | This is the one that catches front-loaded revenue |

**Thresholds.**
- **Trend:** DSO or DIO rising more than about 15 days a year for 2+ years while revenue grows (flag #5 in `insight:forensic-redflag-checklist`).
- **Level:** compare with peers and with the business model. An FMCG company should run a negative CCC, a jeweller about 150–250 days, an EPC company 60–150 days with advances netted.
- **Divergence:** receivables growth more than 1.5x revenue growth.

**Worked example E: PC Jeweller (PCJEWELLER). A working-capital death spiral.**

| | FY18 | FY19 | FY20 | FY21 | FY22 | FY24 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | 9,610 | 8,672 | 5,206 | 2,825 | 1,605 | 604 |
| PAT | 536 | 1 | 83 | 62 | −391 | −629 |
| CFO | 358 | **−1,931** | 76 | 91 | −719 | 64 |
| Inventory days | 232 | 227 | 434 | 954 | 1,465 | **3,044** |
| Payable days | 160 | **57** | 87 | 150 | 4 | 7 |
| Borrowings | 1,116 | 2,121 | 2,429 | 2,414 | 3,391 | 4,150 |

- In FY19, payable days collapsed from 160 to 57: suppliers (gold-metal-loan lenders) stopped extending credit.
- The ₹1,931 cr CFO outflow was funded with ₹1,005 cr of new borrowings. Inventory never turned back into cash.
- **Signal:** the first year payables fall while inventory stays flat is the moment trade creditors have lost confidence. Creditors often know before shareholders do.

**Worked example F: Hindustan Unilever (HINDUNILVR). What "good" looks like.**
- CCC ran between −50 and −107 days over FY15–FY26 (FY26: −89).
- Suppliers and distributors fund the business, so growth releases cash.
- The test for an FMCG company is whether the CCC is **deteriorating**, not where its level sits.
title: course › 2.1 The day counts

body:
- **Sourcing split:** ~40% of purchases are **direct imports** (FIVE is importer of record) and ~60% come from **domestic vendors**. China is the largest source *for both* `[10K25]`. The 10-K gives **no China share** (open item). Calls have not quantified it either `[CC-Q2FY26]`: "not discussed".
- **IEEPA cost revealed by the refund.** The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs in Feb-2026 `[10K25 subsequent event]`. FIVE recorded **$163.6M of IEEPA refunds in Q2 FY26 COGS** (~$170M pre-tax with interest) `[PR-Q2 FY26]`, `[CC-Q2FY26]`.
  - That is ~3.4% of FY25 sales.
  - It implies an effective IEEPA rate of ~20–22% on direct-import FOB [EST: FY25 merchandise cost ~$2.25–2.35B; 40% direct ≈ $0.9B landed; ≈ $0.75B FOB; $164M ÷ $0.75B].
  - FIVE absorbed most of it through FY25 with a **pricing reset**: ticket +5.3% and "price simplification" `[10K25]`, `[CC-Q2FY26]`.
- **Unmodelled second-order effect (nobody asked):** the **domestic-vendor 60%** carried tariffs inside vendor prices. Refunds go to the importer of record, so *vendors* collect those refunds. Does FIVE get any back, through cost renegotiation or vendor allowances? That is a potential further margin tailwind, and a ground-check and IR question. Replacement tariffs under other statutes: "2027 tariffs may be slightly higher" `[CC-Q2FY26]`.
- **Shrink:** FY25 GM benefited from "lower inventory shrinkage" `[10K25]`. Q2 FY26 had an "improved shrink reserve rate". Q3 FY26 faces "an unfavorable shrink comparison against last year's true-up" `[CC-Q2FY26]`. Shrink is accrued between physical counts, so **the true-up quarter moves**. Read the 10-Q MD&A sentence every quarter.
- **Freight and fuel:** "higher fuel cost was absolutely an offset" in Q2. H2 tariff relief is "largely offset" by fuel `[CC-Q2FY26]`. No freight split is disclosed. Proxies: the EIA weekly on-highway diesel price; Drewry WCI / Freightos FBX for Asia–US ocean rates.
- **Price-point architecture:** "most priced at $5 and below". Since the 2025 simplification the language is "most items priced between $1 and $5 and some extreme value items priced beyond $5" `[PR-HOL25]`. The **FY24 10-K risk factor said "price increases (including beyond $5 per item)". FY25 deleted the parenthesis** `[10K24]` vs `[10K25]`. Five Beyond items were moved back into departments, and an "open-wall" reset costs ~$40–45k capex per store `[CC-Q2FY26]`. **The share of sales above $5 is not disclosed.** It is the ground check's main count (§6).

- **Endurance: date reliability.** About half its SOP re-dates were not explained (Chennai, Bajaj, Chinese OEM). FY26 revenue still grew 26%, so this is a forecasting-discipline issue that has not yet shown up in the P&L.
- **Happy Forgings: the INR 650 cr heavy-component plant.** It went from "finished by Q2–Q3 FY27" (Aug-25) to "commence operation in Q4 FY2028" (Nov-26), while each call said "as per schedule". This is the one clearly silent goalpost move on a core project in the set. Its margin promises, by contrast, are the most reliable in the set.
- **Sansera: delivers revenue, misses capacity forecasts.** Group and ADS revenue were met or beaten; capex and the hangar date were not.
- **Sona: few hard promises, delivered or openly revised.** The +50 SAC rests on six records, partly mechanical (non-auto share rose because railways were consolidated). That is why the shrink weight matters.
- **Uniparts (pilot): revenue guidance below peers.** 63% vs Sansera's 100% in the only other revenue ledger. Its capacity and margin records are above peers. With 10 calls and a cycle trough in its window, it is the only company with a full sample.

|---|---|---|---|---|

| debt ≥ 1.5x + negative CFO | 0% vs 1.7% | 70% vs 54% | 10.2% vs 9.0% (FY2018) | 50% vs 34% |
| other income > 30% / > 50% | 2.7% vs 0.7% (> 30%) | 61% vs 48% | 15.5% vs 10.2% (> 30%); 16.9% vs 10.8% (> 50%) | 23% vs 26%; 20% vs 26% |
| ANY | 2.9% vs 1.4% | 64% vs 51% | 13.6% vs 6.1% (FY2018) | 36% vs 34% |

The old Part B said pledged firms tripled *more* often (69% vs 51%, p = 0.006). With dead firms in and the snapshot
not at a market low, pledged firms tripled about **half as often** (15% vs 28%) and lost half their value three
times as often. Even within the live slice of this panel, pledged firms tripled less (20% vs 29%). The old result
was not only survivorship: it came from a COVID-low snapshot plus a sample that admitted small firms only if they
later grew (both biases named there). For the cash-flow rules the direction holds: they fire on winners about as
often as on others (CFO/PAT x3 36% vs 34%; debt + negative CFO 50% vs 34%), which confirms L20.
